The strongest surviving target in this opening is a verified isotope intervention inside an existing covalent structure: change the local mass arrangement, restore the elemental geometry, and independently establish what carbon was transferred. I developed a common force-and-scattering model for that operation. It produces a physically specified mass-readout signal without assigning isotope contrast or reaction probabilities.

The same calculation also weakens the small motif’s materials case. Its most visible predicted vibrational change is largely reproducible by scanning around a stationary isotope. The smaller contribution that depends on the relative arrangement of two labels is substantially harder to measure. I am retaining the mass-transfer witness as the useful opening and withdrawing the small pristine-graphene motif’s optical response as a justification for a material device.

The returning-mediator reachability result, observation limits, processing costs and failed cross-energy calibration remain conditional results at their previous scope. Nothing below supplies the missing carbon-transfer chemistry.

A concrete operation with a paid return and parking path

The proposed intervention uses the retained 24-exchange closed Si route, which returns Si to its starting site while cycling three carbon positions, a,b,fa,b,fa,b,f. For the physical-response calculation, the diagnostic input has 13C^{13}\mathrm C13C at aaa and a fixed spectator position ccc; the other carbons are 12C^{12}\mathrm C12C. The intended output has the heavy labels at f,cf,cf,c.

That input is a specified test configuration, not an acquired preparation or an assumed success probability.

I added an explicit 16-hop Si parking path, ending approximately 2 nm from the intervention region. Its final token permutation has disjoint support from the carbon cycle. This permits the following paired comparison:

  1. Park Si and acquire the first read.
  2. Return Si, perform the closed carbon cycle, and park Si along the same path.
  3. Acquire the second read.

Under faithful exchanges, both read states have the same elemental structure and the same rearrangement along the parking path. Their intended difference is the isotope arrangement in the intervention region.

The exchange counts are consequential:

ComparisonIdeal successful Si–C exchanges
Before/edit/after, ending with Si parked72
Same comparison, followed by returning Si to its initial site88
Before/edit/undo/reference, ending with Si parked128

These counts exclude unsuccessful attempts, recovery, initial isotope identification, registration and imaging. I have not converted them into operating times using the earlier rate calibration, which failed its cross-energy check.

Published work establishes Si–C bond inversion and controlled Si motion as real starting operations. It also establishes competing configurations and pathways. It does not establish that every visually successful Si displacement transports the expected carbon isotope. In particular, an adatom excursion followed by refilling cannot be classified from the final Si position alone. arxiv.org+1

Parking helps separate the reader from the most reactive neighbourhood. It does not by itself establish that the parked Si has negligible mechanical influence, that the entire parking-path inventory survived, or that long spectroscopy exposures are passive.

A mass witness derived from the scattering interaction

The useful readout result is an energy-moment identity.

Let the nuclear Hamiltonian be

H=∑ipi22Mi+V(R),H=\sum_i\frac{\mathbf p_i^2}{2M_i}+V(\mathbf R),H=i∑​2Mi​pi2​​+V(R),

and let A(R)A(\mathbf R)A(R) be the position-dependent electron-scattering operator for a specified incident probe and outgoing detector channel. For a stationary, time-reversal-invariant nuclear state, the full signed nuclear energy-transfer spectrum obeys

∫−∞∞E SA(E) dE=ℏ22∑i⟨∣∇iA∣2⟩Mi.\boxed{ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} E\,S_A(E)\,dE = \frac{\hbar^2}{2} \sum_i \frac{\left\langle|\nabla_i A|^2\right\rangle}{M_i}. }∫−∞∞​ESA​(E)dE=2ℏ2​i∑​Mi​⟨∣∇i​A∣2⟩​.​

The integral includes energy gain, energy loss and all phonon orders. It is not the centroid of an arbitrarily selected optical-phonon peak.

This separates two roles of spectroscopy:

  • The full nuclear energy moment can constrain the mass distribution.
  • The distribution of that scattering across vibrational energies probes the material’s dynamics.

The potential VVV cancels from the explicit double commutator. It does not disappear from a focused-probe experiment: the thermal average of ∣∇iA∣2|\nabla_i A|^2∣∇i​A∣2 depends on the nuclear position distribution. Consequently, this is not a force-model-free, single-atom mass oracle.

I also completed the second-moment calculation for the thermal harmonic model. Writing g=∇Ag=\nabla Ag=∇A, with CvC_vCv​ the velocity covariance and mμm_\mumμ​ the mass associated with coordinate μ\muμ,

M2=ℏ2⟨g†Cvg⟩+ℏ44∑μ,ν⟨∣∂μ∂νA∣2⟩mμmν.M_2 = \hbar^2\left\langle g^\dagger C_vg\right\rangle + \frac{\hbar^4}{4} \sum_{\mu,\nu} \frac{ \left\langle |\partial_\mu\partial_\nu A|^2 \right\rangle }{ m_\mu m_\nu }.M2​=ℏ2⟨g†Cv​g⟩+4ℏ4​μ,ν∑​mμ​mν​⟨∣∂μ​∂ν​A∣2⟩​.

This supplies the fluctuation cost from the same scattering operator. No Gaussian recoil-line shape or independently selected isotope contrast is needed. I checked the moment expressions against an explicit thermal quantum-oscillator calculation.

The underlying recoil-readout idea is prior art. Argentero and colleagues already proposed isotope identification through high-angle electron energy transfer and examined its counting requirements; their initial experiment distinguished gold and carbon, rather than demonstrating single-12C^{12}\mathrm C12C/13C^{13}\mathrm C13C identification. The contribution here is the calculation for a finite coherent probe, finite detector and the retained transfer operation. arxiv.org

What the common physical model actually contains

The carbon calculation uses the published Perebeinos–Tersoff valence-force model, with the same force matrix before and after the mass rearrangement. I used its in-plane harmonic terms, a 300 K thermal state, and periodic cells of 288 and 800 atoms. The main parameters were taken directly from the paper; a second published parameter fit supplied a check on the predicted local response. This force model describes carbon vibrations, not reactive Si–C chemistry. arxiv.org

The electron calculation uses a coherent incident pupil and the published Lobato–Van Dyck neutral-carbon scattering factor. Thus the mass-sensitive signal and the vibrational scattering weights arise from an electron–atom interaction, rather than from an assigned measurement channel. nano.uantwerpen.be

The specified ideal reader has:

  • 60 keV incident electrons;
  • a 32 mrad convergence semi-angle;
  • a circular detector with a 12 mrad semi-angle, centred at a chosen 110 mrad offset;
  • 28 meV energy-resolution FWHM;
  • unit detection efficiency.

The convergence, collection aperture, resolution and approximately 7 pA current are grounded in published single-atom vibrational spectroscopy. The 110 mrad offset and ideal aberration-free pupil are calculation choices; I am not attributing that complete configuration to the published experiment. In particular, the reported 5.8 meV on-axis resolution cannot be substituted for the 28 meV off-axis resolution while retaining the rest of this calculation. n11.iphy.ac.cn

The model includes nuclear thermal motion, coherent probe amplitudes, detector weighting and the isotope-dependent normal modes. It omits out-of-plane motion, reactive Si interactions, electronic inelastic background, actual probe aberrations and detector inefficiency. Translation modes are excluded in the finite-cell covariance calculation. Those qualifications prevent its numerical output from becoming an experimentally calibrated reader.

Predicted mass and material signals

For the two-label test configuration, the calculated changes are:

Probe positionIntended local isotope changeChange in full nuclear energy momentChange in optical-band centroid
aaa13C→12C^{13}\mathrm C\rightarrow{}^{12}\mathrm C13C→12Cabout +7.8%about +2.05 meV
fff12C→13C^{12}\mathrm C\rightarrow{}^{13}\mathrm C12C→13Cabout −7.2%about −2.09 meV
bbbremains 12C^{12}\mathrm C12Cabout +0.08%about +0.677 meV

The last column is the centroid of the calculated one-phonon electron-scattering component, convolved with the stated resolution and integrated over 145–210 meV. It is not a prediction for an unprocessed experimental spectrum containing all backgrounds and multiphonon contributions.

The distinction at bbb is useful: its own isotope stays fixed, its mass-sensitive moment changes very little, and its optical response changes because its neighbourhood changes. Before applying electron-scattering weights, the local projected vibrational density of states gave a shift of approximately +0.57+0.57+0.57 to +0.62+0.62+0.62 meV across the two published force-model fits. Applying the coherent scattering weights gives approximately +0.677+0.677+0.677 meV in the main model. Increasing the angular quadrature changed that result by roughly 0.00010.00010.0001 meV; numerical integration is not its dominant uncertainty.

This establishes a conditional discriminating prediction. It does not establish a new materials advantage.

The stronger conventional comparison changes the interpretation

A stationary isotope already produces a spatially varying vibrational response. In a translationally uniform sheet, moving one isotope and holding the probe fixed can be equivalent to holding the isotope fixed and moving the probe. A writer cannot claim that response as an advantage over an ordinary spatial scan.

I therefore repeated the electron-scattering calculation with only the moving label present.

At the unchanged probe site bbb:

ΔEˉtwo labels=0.6766 meV,\Delta \bar E_{\text{two labels}} =0.6766\ \mathrm{meV},ΔEˉtwo labels​=0.6766 meV,

whereas

ΔEˉsingle label=0.7364 meV.\Delta \bar E_{\text{single label}} =0.7364\ \mathrm{meV}.ΔEˉsingle label​=0.7364 meV.

Most of the visible change therefore survives without the second retained label. The approximately −0.060-0.060−0.060 meV difference between those centroid changes is much smaller.

Because centroids are nonlinear normalizations, I also compared the unnormalized spectra. The appropriate connected difference is

ΔSconn(E)=[Sfc(E)−Sac(E)]−[Sf(E)−Sa(E)].\Delta S_{\rm conn}(E) = \big[S_{fc}(E)-S_{ac}(E)\big] - \big[S_f(E)-S_a(E)\big].ΔSconn​(E)=[Sfc​(E)−Sac​(E)]−[Sf​(E)−Sa​(E)].

It vanishes for a strictly additive response of independent isotope labels. In this model it does not vanish, but it is small.

An optimally weighted linear comparison of the four ideal one-phonon spectra, using only their counting noise in the 145–210 meV window, requires approximately

2.9×10122.9\times10^{12}2.9×1012

primary electrons per spectrum for the diagnostic separation criterion used here. At 7 pA, that is about 18 hours per spectrum, or about 74 hours for four spectra. This remains a favourable model calculation: background, drift, imperfect preparation and structural survival are additional costs.

That is the decisive negative result for the present material motif. The calculation supports a local spectral effect, but the part that specifically tests the interaction of the two retained labels is expensive relative to what the simpler spatial-scan comparison already supplies. It does not justify calling this a useful phononic device.

The broader incumbents are also substantial:

FunctionIndependently effective alternativeRemaining distinction of the proposed operation
Change graphene’s isotopic composition and thermal propertiesCVD-grown isotope-engineered regions, including different compositions within one sheetEditing an already assembled atomic neighbourhood
Produce correlated isotope arrangementsLabelled molecular precursors producing carbon nanotubes with evidence consistent with 13C^{13}\mathrm C13C-rich clustersSelecting and reversibly changing a particular local arrangement
Identify isotope distributions in grapheneAtomic-scale vibrational isotope imaging and diffusion measurementsCertifying the outcome of a particular manipulation sequence
Identify and reposition individual isotopesESR-STM identification and reversible movement of individual Ti isotopes on MgOTransferring host atoms within an existing covalent network

These alternatives are realized capabilities or experimentally supported constructions, not ideal comparators granted free assembly or readout. arxiv.org+3

Single-isotope perturbations of spatial vibrational spectra also have explicit first-principles precedent. The possible new operation lies in controlled post-assembly intervention and verification, not in the existence of an isotope-dependent vibrational response. PubMed

The mass witness survives, with substantial physical costs

For a before/after mass-moment measurement at a changed site, the calculation gives a diagnostic requirement of approximately

8.9×1098.9\times10^98.9×109

primary electrons for each spectrum. At 7 pA this is approximately 3.4 minutes per spectrum. Reading both changed positions before and after therefore takes approximately 13.5 minutes of ideal beam time.

The associated peak fluence is approximately

1.2×1010 electrons/A˚21.2\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{electrons/\mathring A^2}1.2×1010 electrons/A˚2

per spectrum.

This estimate uses a variance bound within the specified model and a normal-approximation separation criterion. It is neither a calibrated 99% experimental identification probability nor a fundamental minimum dose.

The ordinary 0.6770.6770.677 meV optical-centroid comparison at bbb is more expensive: approximately 4.3×10104.3\times10^{10}4.3×1010 primary electrons, or 16 minutes, for each of the two ideal spectra. Thus even the readily visible model response entails appreciable exposure.

Published recoil-readout work reports routine pristine-graphene stability around 108 electrons/A˚210^8\ \mathrm{electrons/\mathring A^2}108 electrons/A˚2 under its conditions, while explicitly allowing that stability could extend further. That is not a destruction threshold. It also does not establish survival through the larger exposures calculated here. arxiv.org

Three interfaces remain particularly important.

The energy window must contain the observable being used

In a harmonic self-scattering benchmark at the central momentum transfer, restricting the nuclear spectrum to ∣E∣<0.3|E|<0.3∣E∣<0.3 eV misses approximately 8% of its first energy moment. That is comparable to the isotope signal itself.

Expanding to ∣E∣<0.8|E|<0.8∣E∣<0.8 eV reduces the missing moment to approximately 10−510^{-5}10−5 in that benchmark. This is a central-momentum self-scattering result, not a bound for the whole focused-probe experiment.

A wider window introduces a need to establish the electronic background and its fluctuations. A background that cancels in a mean difference can still contribute substantial noise. The published spectra and source workbooks I inspected provide useful phonon shapes and relative intensities, but do not provide the absolute detector statistics needed to close this calculation.

Therefore a plotted optical spectrum cannot simply be integrated and declared a mass measurement.

Energy referencing is part of the operation

An energy-origin error δE\delta EδE changes the measured first moment by

δM1=δE M0,\delta M_1=\delta E\,M_0,δM1​=δEM0​,

where M0M_0M0​ is the collected nuclear scattering intensity.

Using the deliberately loose intensity bound from the calculation, keeping this bias below one-tenth of the isotope signal would correspond to an energy-origin error near 0.030.030.03 meV. That number is not a universal instrumental requirement: the bound is loose, and shared reference measurements can cancel common offsets.

For example,

M1,aM0,f−M1,fM0,aM_{1,a}M_{0,f}-M_{1,f}M_{0,a}M1,a​M0,f​−M1,f​M0,a​

cancels an exactly common energy offset algebraically. But actual intensity normalization, angle-dependent distortions and time-dependent drift still have to be established. The algebra does not supply their calibration.

Parking must be judged by accumulated halo dose

The relevant exposure of the parked reactive neighbourhood is

Λpark=∑jσj∫Φj(t) dt,\Lambda_{\rm park} = \sum_j \sigma_j\int \Phi_j(t)\,dt,Λpark​=j∑​σj​∫Φj​(t)dt,

not simply the distance between the probe maximum and Si.

The ideal pupil used here admits a small-halo window for the explicit parking path. That is encouraging within the model. It is not transferable to an actual microscope from its nominal probe width alone. A published graphene experiment found substantial broad probe tails and less than 21% of the integrated beam intensity within the probe FWHM; transformations frequently occurred while the beam maximum was away from the defect. Nature Communications

A measured intensity profile is also insufficient to reconstruct the complete coherent probe phase used by the read calculation.

What this changes about the carbon-transfer question

The useful prospective operation is now more precise:

Use a returned-mediator cycle to attempt a local isotope rearrangement, then test the resulting mass distribution independently of the Si-position record.

If acquired, that readout would allow functional mass transfer to be accepted without requiring every microscopic trajectory to preserve the identity of the same carbon atom. An excursion followed by recovery of the correct isotope could be acceptable for a mass-patterning function. A visually identical endpoint produced by wrong-isotope refilling would fail.

That distinction matters because the published direct-exchange trajectory and the competing adatom/refilling pathways are not interchangeable evidence. Their existence does not provide the conditional probabilities of correct transfer, own-atom recapture, wrong-isotope replacement or irreversible loss in the intended operation. I have not supplied those probabilities. arxiv.org

There is an additional scope limit: reading a,b,fa,b,fa,b,f would certify only the tested local output, subject to calibration. It would not certify the complete isotope inventory along every visited site. The explicit closed route plus parking path visits a substantially larger region. A full inventory claim would require additional observations, with extra exposure and special difficulty near the parked Si. Those costs cannot be hidden inside a three-site acceptance test.

Likewise, the finite carbon force model does not show that the remote Si contribution cancels exactly. Returning it to the same position removes a direct change of elemental geometry between the two reads, but its presence can still modify the sensitivity to the isotope intervention. Out-of-plane motion, support conditions and the actual Si–C force field must enter a quantitative prediction for the assembled system.

Scientific choice at this checkpoint

I would sustain this opening around certified carbon flow and reversible local isotope intervention, with the mass witness as the enabling uncertainty. I would not invest the next extended unit in a larger permutation construction or in refining this small motif’s optical centroid.

The completed work establishes four things:

  • A source-based carbon force model and a finite coherent electron probe produce isotope information without an assigned contrast function.
  • The same model predicts a distinct response at an atom whose own mass stays unchanged.
  • A stronger static-label comparison reproduces most of that response, sharply reducing its present materials significance.
  • Full-spectrum collection, energy referencing, accumulated exposure and unverified reaction branches remain consequential parts of the operation.

The attractive capability remains a controlled intervention in one existing covalent neighbourhood, with an independent record of its mass outcome. The present calculation makes that capability testable and exposes its costs. It does not yet establish a usable isotope writer, a thermal-material advantage, or reliable carbon-transfer chemistry.

What this changes about the carbon-transfer question

The useful prospective operation is now more precise:

Use a returned-mediator cycle to attempt a local isotope rearrangement, then test the resulting mass distribution independently of the Si-position record.

If acquired, that readout would allow functional mass transfer to be accepted without requiring every microscopic trajectory to preserve the identity of the same carbon atom. An excursion followed by recovery of the correct isotope could be acceptable for a mass-patterning function. A visually identical endpoint produced by wrong-isotope refilling would fail.

That distinction matters because the published direct-exchange trajectory and the competing adatom/refilling pathways are not interchangeable evidence. Their existence does not provide the conditional probabilities of correct transfer, own-atom recapture, wrong-isotope replacement or irreversible loss in the intended operation. I have not supplied those probabilities.

Scientific choice at this checkpoint

I would sustain this opening around certified carbon flow and reversible local isotope intervention, with the mass witness as the enabling uncertainty. I would not invest the next extended unit in a larger permutation construction or in refining this small motif’s optical centroid.

The completed work establishes four things:

A source-based carbon force model and a finite coherent electron probe produce isotope information without an assigned contrast function.
The same model predicts a distinct response at an atom whose own mass stays unchanged.
A stronger static-label comparison reproduces most of that response, sharply reducing its present materials significance.
Full-spectrum collection, energy referencing, accumulated exposure and unverified reaction branches remain consequential parts of the operation.

The attractive capability remains a controlled intervention in one existing covalent neighbourhood, with an independent record of its mass outcome. The present calculation makes that capability testable and exposes its costs. It does not yet establish a usable isotope writer, a thermal-material advantage, or reliable carbon-transfer chemistry.
